concepts.description: What atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability actually guarantee — a transaction is an abstraction that collapses partial failure into commit-or-abort.
concepts.title: ACID Transactions

concepts.description: A hierarchical alternative to flat scatter/gather — parent nodes merge and rank leaf results at each level, bounding fan-in and spreading aggregation work instead of concentrating it at one coordinator.
concepts.title: Aggregation Trees

concepts.description: Run-to-completion compute optimized for aggregate throughput versus long-lived request handlers optimized for per-request latency — different failure and scaling shapes on the same fleet.
concepts.title: Batch versus Serving Jobs

concepts.description: A process that blocks its own initialization on a synchronous remote call turns an unresponsive dependency into a deployment-wide restart loop, not just one slow request.
concepts.title: Blocking Startup Dependencies

concepts.description: The fault model where nodes may lie or act maliciously — expensive to tolerate, and usually the wrong model for private datacenters.
concepts.title: Byzantine Faults

concepts.description: Memory-speed read tiers in front of a datastore: the population-strategy choices, the staleness/divergence risks each carries, and the thundering herd failure mode.
concepts.title: Caching Tiers

concepts.description: When a network partition occurs, a replicated system must choose between linearizable consistency and availability — better read as "consistent or available when partitioned".
concepts.title: CAP Theorem

concepts.description: How one node's failure spreads: load shifted onto survivors kills them in sequence, and blocked synchronous callers propagate a downstream failure upstream — with slow responses worse than outright death.
concepts.title: Cascading Failures

concepts.description: The consistency model in which all observers see causes before effects — a partial order over operations, and the strongest model that stays available and fast under network partitions.
concepts.title: Causal Ordering

concepts.description: Partitioning a system into multiple independent, equivalent copies (cells) so a single event's blast radius is bounded to one copy instead of the whole fleet.
concepts.title: Cell-Based Isolation (Failure Domains)

concepts.description: Extracting a database's write stream from its replication log and feeding it to derived systems, making search indexes, caches, and warehouses followers of the system of record.
concepts.title: Change Data Capture (CDC)

concepts.description: Waiting out the assumed maximum clock skew across a cluster before exposing a write (or, cheaper, restarting a read that lands in the uncertainty window) so timestamp order matches real-time order everywhere.
concepts.title: Clock-Bound Wait

concepts.description: A region groups nearby datacenters for latency and data-residency reasons; its availability zones are engineered so a failure in one has negligible chance of also taking down another.
concepts.title: Cloud Regions and Availability Zones

concepts.description: Getting nodes to irrevocably agree on a value despite crashes and network faults — the primitive behind leader election, atomic commit, and replicated logs.
concepts.title: Consensus

concepts.description: The guarantee that readers observe writes in an order that respects causality — never an answer before its question.
concepts.title: Consistent Prefix Reads

concepts.description: How a log-based broker divides a topic's partitions among a consumer group's members without a lock service — deterministic assignment computed independently by each consumer, re-run whenever membership changes.
concepts.title: Consumer Group Rebalancing

concepts.description: A globally distributed edge-caching layer that serves content from wherever demand is, populated on first request rather than pre-replicated everywhere, colocated inside ISPs to cut transit cost.
concepts.title: Content Delivery Networks

concepts.description: The layer that provisions, configures, and reroutes a fleet is a separate failure domain from the layer that serves requests — and because it acts on the whole fleet at once, its automation has a far larger blast radius.
concepts.title: Control Plane versus Data Plane

concepts.description: Many business "constraints" are actually loose — violations can be apologized for and compensated — which lets systems skip synchronous consensus for throughput, latency, and cross-region availability.
concepts.title: Coordination Avoidance

concepts.description: ZooKeeper/etcd-style replicated in-memory key-value stores exposing consensus as linearizable primitives: locks, leases, leader election, membership, and watches.
concepts.title: Coordination Services

concepts.description: L4 vs. L7 proxy tiers between applications and datastores — read/write splitting, lag-aware routing, and failover redirection, at the cost of a new critical component.
concepts.title: Database Proxies

concepts.description: Inside the datacenter, RPC clients balance directly across backend tasks — deterministic subsetting tames the connection mesh, and load-aware picking beats round robin.
concepts.title: Datacenter Load Balancing

concepts.description: A secondary queue that receives messages a primary queue's workers cannot process after a bounded number of attempts — stopping infinite retry loops while preserving failed messages for inspection.
concepts.title: Dead-Letter Queues

concepts.description: Making periodic job scheduling fault-tolerant: consensus-elected leader, replicated schedule state, decoupled execution, and idempotent jobs to absorb duplicates and catch-ups.
concepts.title: Distributed Cron

concepts.description: Mutual exclusion across nodes via time-limited leases from a linearizable service — only safe when paired with receiver-side fencing.
concepts.title: Distributed Locks and Leases

concepts.description: Application code writing the same change to two systems (database plus cache/index) inevitably drifts via race conditions and partial failure — the motivation for log-based integration.
concepts.title: The Dual Writes Problem

concepts.description: Workers pull work from a shared pool of small chunks instead of owning fixed partitions — bounding how much progress a single worker death loses.
concepts.title: Dynamic Work Assignment

concepts.description: "Exactly-once" semantics in stream processing: faults cause reprocessing, but atomic offset+state+output commits or idempotent writes make the net effect appear once.
concepts.title: Effectively-Once Delivery

concepts.description: Picking the oldest live cluster member as coordinator with no formal election or quorum, trading a real risk of split brain for never being unavailable.
concepts.title: Emergent Leader

concepts.description: Low-level reliability mechanisms (TCP, transactions, exactly-once processing) cannot guarantee application correctness; deduplication and integrity need an identifier carried end to end.
concepts.title: The End-to-End Argument

concepts.description: Managed-compute workers treated as interchangeable cattle — any instance may be killed and replaced by the scheduler without human intervention, which requires stamp-out automation and off-machine state.
concepts.title: Ephemeral Compute Instances

concepts.description: Storing application state as an append-only log of immutable domain events and deriving current state by replay — the state/stream duality made explicit.
concepts.title: Event Sourcing and Immutable Logs

concepts.description: The weak guarantee that replicas converge to the same value once writes stop — with no promise about when, or what reads return in the meantime.
concepts.title: Eventual Consistency

concepts.description: Splitting a shared-schema change into add-then-dual-write-then-remove phases so a rolling deploy never requires old and new application code to agree on a single instantaneous cutover.
concepts.title: Expand-Contract Schema Migration

concepts.description: One incoming write triggering many derived writes (or one read triggering many backend calls) — the Twitter-timeline trade between write-time materialization and read-time assembly.
concepts.title: Fan-Out

concepts.description: Monotonically increasing tokens issued with each lease or lock grant, letting the protected resource itself reject writes from deposed zombie leaders.
concepts.title: Fencing Tokens

concepts.description: Decoupling a key's logical partition from its physical node by fixing the partition count independently of cluster size, so adding nodes rebalances ownership without reshuffling every key's assignment.
concepts.title: Fixed Partitions

concepts.description: Routing read-only traffic to the nearest or least-loaded follower to offload the leader, and the mechanisms that bound how stale an answer a client is willing to accept.
concepts.title: Follower Reads

concepts.description: A monotonically increasing number bumped on every leadership change and tagged onto every log entry and request, so nodes can tell which of two conflicting entries or leaders is authoritative.
concepts.title: Generation Clock

concepts.description: The frontend traffic stack at global scale: geo-DNS steers coarsely, anycast plus consistent-hashing L4 balancers spread packets, and L7 proxies route requests with capacity-aware overflow between datacenters.
concepts.title: Global Load Balancing Tiers

concepts.description: Spreading metadata across a large cluster by having each node periodically exchange everything it knows with one random peer, converging in time proportional to log(n) without an all-to-all message pattern.
concepts.title: Gossip Dissemination

concepts.description: Two operations are concurrent when neither knew about the other; causality (happened-before), not wall-clock time, is what defines conflicts and ordering in distributed systems.
concepts.title: Happens-Before and Concurrency

concepts.description: Assigning keys to partitions by hash to spread load uniformly — at the cost of destroying key-order locality and range queries.
concepts.title: Hash Partitioning

concepts.description: Periodically sending a liveness message to peers so absence of the message, not just a slow response, is what a timeout is measured against.
concepts.title: Heartbeat

concepts.description: The log index confirmed replicated to a quorum of followers, below which entries are safe to apply and serve — nothing beyond it may ever be exposed to a client.
concepts.title: High Water Mark

concepts.description: Disproportionate load on one partition or node — from key ordering, unfair splits, or single hot keys — which collapses a cluster's throughput to that of one node.
concepts.title: Hot Spots and Skew

concepts.description: A (wall-clock time, tick counter) timestamp that is monotonic and causality-preserving like a Lamport timestamp, but stays anchored to real date-time so versions can be queried "as of" an actual moment.
concepts.title: Hybrid Clock

concepts.description: Making an operation safe to apply multiple times with the effect of once — the property that makes retries safe on a network where success is unknowable.
concepts.title: Idempotency

concepts.description: A replicated master dynamically assigns contiguous key ranges to worker machines and moves, splits, or merges them under load — partition rebalancing applied to a stateful stream-processing computation instead of a storage cluster.
concepts.title: Key Interval Load Balancing

concepts.description: Assigning continuous ranges of sorted keys to partitions — efficient range scans, but monotonically increasing keys create write hot spots.
concepts.title: Key-Range Partitioning

concepts.description: Transport-level balancers push packets cheaply but blindly; application- level balancers see requests and can route on content — the throughput versus intelligence trade at every tier.
concepts.title: L4 vs. L7 Load Balancing

concepts.description: A (counter, node ID) pair maintained by max-and-increment on every message, giving a total order of events consistent with causality — but only after the fact.
concepts.title: Lamport Timestamps

concepts.description: Conflict resolution that keeps only the write with the highest timestamp — convergent, but silently discards concurrent writes and is corrupted by clock skew.
concepts.title: Last Write Wins (LWW)

concepts.description: How a cluster actually picks a leader — in-process voting for small consensus clusters versus delegating to an external linearizable store for large ones — and why quorum reads/writes alone can't substitute for it.
concepts.title: Leader Election Mechanics

concepts.description: Promoting a follower to leader after the leader fails — a process riddled with pitfalls: lost writes, reused primary keys, and split-brain.
concepts.title: Leader Failover

concepts.description: Dynamo-style replication with no leader: clients send reads and writes to several replicas in parallel and rely on quorum overlap, read repair, and anti-entropy for consistency.
concepts.title: Leaderless Replication

concepts.description: The recency guarantee that a replicated system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data, with every operation atomic at one point in a single global timeline.
concepts.title: Linearizability

concepts.description: Brokers (Kafka, Kinesis) that store each topic partition as a durable append-only log with per-message offsets — ordered, replayable consumption instead of destructive reads.
concepts.title: Log-Based Message Brokers

concepts.description: The read-modify-write race where a later write overwrites a concurrent update without incorporating it — and the spectrum of fixes from atomic operations to compare-and-set.
concepts.title: Lost Updates

concepts.description: The log index below which a write-ahead log's entries are safe to discard, computed either from a durable state snapshot or from an age-based retention window.
concepts.title: Low Water Mark

concepts.description: Agreeing on which nodes are currently alive members of a cluster — a consensus decision, because failure detection alone cannot produce an agreed answer.
concepts.title: Membership Services

concepts.description: How messages travel between services — direct messaging, transient AMQP-style brokers, and log-based brokers — and the ordering and loss semantics each implies.
concepts.title: Message Brokers and Delivery Semantics

concepts.description: Measuring lag and detecting silent replica divergence — replication can break without erroring, so freshness and consistency must be actively verified.
concepts.title: Monitoring Replication Health

concepts.description: The guarantee that a user's successive reads never move backward in time — once a value is seen, an older state is never returned.
concepts.title: Monotonic Reads

concepts.description: Replication design where several nodes accept writes independently and replicate asynchronously to each other, trading write conflicts for local write latency and partition tolerance.
concepts.title: Multi-Leader Replication

concepts.description: The defining hazard of distributed systems: some components fail nondeterministically while the rest keep working, so the system is never simply "up" or "down".
concepts.title: Partial Failure

concepts.description: Secondary indexes don't align with primary-key partitions; the choice is local indexes (cheap writes, scatter/gather reads) versus global term-partitioned indexes (cheap reads, distributed writes).
concepts.title: Partitioned Secondary Indexes

concepts.description: Splitting a dataset so each record belongs to exactly one partition, spreading storage and load across a shared-nothing cluster.
concepts.title: Partitioning (Sharding)

concepts.description: The two-phase (prepare, accept) protocol for reaching agreement on a single value without a stable leader, and why real systems build a replicated log on top of it rather than run it directly.
concepts.title: Paxos

concepts.description: A single server's request capacity is bounded by four physical resources — CPU, memory, network, disk — and distribution exists to give a workload physically separate copies of each.
concepts.title: Physical Resource Limits as the Root Cause of Distribution

concepts.description: A thread can be preempted for seconds or minutes at any point without knowing it, invalidating any local belief about time, leases, or leadership.
concepts.title: Process Pauses

concepts.description: Whether a sender forwards data to a consumer as soon as it's available or a consumer requests it at its own pace — pull gives the consumer natural flow control and a free replay position, at the cost of poll latency.
concepts.title: Push vs. Pull Consumption

concepts.description: Placing a message queue between a fast producer and a rate- or capacity-limited consumer decouples their speeds and lets you tune worker parallelism to protect downstream systems.
concepts.title: Queue as Load Buffer

concepts.description: The w + r > n condition ensuring read and write replica sets overlap in at least one up-to-date node — and the edge cases where the overlap still returns stale data.
concepts.title: Quorum Reads and Writes

concepts.description: The baseline isolation level: no dirty reads (only committed data is seen) and no dirty writes (only committed data is overwritten).
concepts.title: Read Committed Isolation

concepts.description: Indexes, caches, and materialized views shift work between eager write-time computation and lazy read-time computation — a boundary that can extend all the way to end-user devices.
concepts.title: Read Path and Write Path

concepts.description: The two mechanisms leaderless systems use to bring stale replicas up to date: fixing staleness observed during reads, and background comparison of replica contents.
concepts.title: Read Repair and Anti-Entropy

concepts.description: After metadata lookup returns candidate replicas, how the client picks which copy to read — local preference, rack locality, and randomization among ties determine load spread.
concepts.title: Read Replica Selection

concepts.description: The guarantee that a user who submits a write will see that write on subsequent reads, despite reading from lagging replicas.
concepts.title: Read-Your-Writes Consistency

concepts.description: Moving partitions between nodes as the cluster grows, shrinks, or fails — minimizing data movement while keeping load fair, and the case for a human in the loop.
concepts.title: Rebalancing Partitions

concepts.description: A general availability spectrum — how synchronized a standby is with the active node trades recovery speed against the runtime cost of keeping it current, from millisecond hot failover to power-on-reset cold failover.
concepts.title: Redundant Spare Tiers: Hot, Warm, and Cold

concepts.description: Keeping every node's state identical by agreeing on a write-ahead log entry-by-entry and applying entries in that same order everywhere — the concrete mechanics Raft and Multi-Paxos use in steady state.
concepts.title: Replicated Log

concepts.description: The delay between a write on the leader and its appearance on asynchronous followers, which turns "scale reads with replicas" into a source of consistency anomalies.
concepts.title: Replication Lag

concepts.description: The four ways a leader can represent changes for followers — statement-based, WAL shipping, logical (row-based), and trigger-based — and what each breaks.
concepts.title: Replication Log Implementations

concepts.description: Coalescing several requests into one network call amortizes fixed per-request overhead, but retrying a partially-applied batch is only safe if the receiver deduplicates.
concepts.title: Request Batching and Idempotency

concepts.description: Sending the next request before the previous response arrives, to stop a single-socket channel from sitting idle between round trips — and the reordering hazard that pipelining introduces under retry.
concepts.title: Request Pipeline

concepts.description: How a client's request finds the node currently owning a key's partition — forwarding between nodes, a routing tier, or partition-aware clients, with placement metadata agreed via a coordination service.
concepts.title: Request Routing to Partitions

concepts.description: Correlating asynchronously arriving peer responses back to the client request that triggered them, and firing a callback once a completion criterion such as quorum is met.
concepts.title: Request Waiting List

concepts.description: Retries convert transient distributed faults into success — or multiply an outage: bound them, back off exponentially with jitter, and retry only what is safe and worth retrying.
concepts.title: Retry Design

concepts.description: A rolling deploy puts old and new code on the wire and on disk at the same time, so every encoding a distributed system uses must stay both backward and forward compatible across that window.
concepts.title: Rolling Upgrade Compatibility

concepts.description: Bigger machine versus shared-nothing cluster — and why the real dividing line is state: stateless tiers distribute trivially, stateful data systems buy every distribution problem at once.
concepts.title: Scale-Up vs. Scale-Out

concepts.description: A named framework distinguishing three orthogonal ways to add capacity — replicate everything, split by function, or split by data — and when each one is the right move to reach for.
concepts.title: Three Axes of Scaling (the AKF Cube)

concepts.description: Mechanisms that work at small node counts and break at large ones: point-to-point meshes grow O(N²), and shared central resources become the bottleneck every added node deepens.
concepts.title: Scaling Effects

concepts.description: Splitting a write-ahead log into multiple size-bounded files instead of one unbounded file, so old data can be identified and deleted in whole units.
concepts.title: Segmented Log

concepts.description: The strongest isolation level — outcomes equal to some serial execution — and its three implementations: actual serial execution, two-phase locking, and serializable snapshot isolation.
concepts.title: Serializability

concepts.description: How callers find current, healthy instances of a service — from static config and DNS (with its caching traps) to dynamic registries and floating VIPs.
concepts.title: Service Discovery

concepts.description: A sidecar proxy co-deployed with every service instance to handle interservice communication, splitting a fleet-wide control plane for routing/security policy from a per-instance data plane that enforces it.
concepts.title: Service Mesh

concepts.description: Replication design where one node (the leader) accepts all writes and streams ordered change logs to followers, which serve read-only queries.
concepts.title: Single-Leader Replication

concepts.description: Routing all communication between a pair of nodes through one long-lived TCP connection, relying on TCP's own ordering instead of building message ordering at the application layer.
concepts.title: Single Socket Channel

concepts.description: Funnel concurrent callers through one queue drained by exactly one worker thread, so state mutation stays single-threaded and correct without blocking callers on slow work like disk writes.
concepts.title: Singular Update Queue

concepts.description: Accepting writes on reachable non-home replicas during a partition, then forwarding them home later — better write availability at the cost of the quorum overlap guarantee.
concepts.title: Sloppy Quorum and Hinted Handoff

concepts.description: Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database at its start time, implemented by keeping multiple versions of every object (MVCC); readers and writers never block each other.
concepts.title: Snapshot Isolation and MVCC

concepts.description: The failure mode where two nodes simultaneously believe they are the leader and both accept writes, causing conflicting or lost data.
concepts.title: Split-Brain

concepts.description: Serving reads directly from a leader's local state to skip replication overhead is unsafe when the leader has been silently partitioned away and doesn't yet know it was deposed.
concepts.title: Stale-Leader Read Hazard

concepts.description: Keeping replicas identical by feeding the same deterministic operations, in the same order, to every replica — the log is the system's ground truth.
concepts.title: State Machine Replication

concepts.description: Pushing change notifications to subscribed clients over an existing connection instead of making them poll, and the harder problem of not losing events across a disconnect.
concepts.title: State Watch

concepts.description: Keeping per-request history out of service instances makes any instance interchangeable; when statefulness can't be avoided, pinning a client to one instance trades that interchangeability for simplicity.
concepts.title: Stateless Services and Session Affinity

concepts.description: Per-key hooks that fire on wall-clock time or on watermark progress, journaled for durability and guaranteed to fire in increasing timestamp order with the same exactly-once guarantee as ordinary records.
concepts.title: Stream Processing Timers

concepts.description: A per-computation bound on the timestamps of records still to arrive, defined recursively over the dataflow graph and computed by aggregating every worker's in-flight and persisted state through a sharded, journaled central authority.
concepts.title: Stream Processing Watermarks

concepts.description: The trade-off between waiting for follower confirmation on every write (durability, but blocked by any slow follower) and confirming immediately (responsive, but recent writes are lost if the leader dies).
concepts.title: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Replication

concepts.description: The formal assumptions about timing and node failure under which a distributed algorithm's correctness is defined and proved.
concepts.title: System Models

concepts.description: Fanning a request out to many backends means overall latency is gated by the slowest one, so a small per-node tail probability becomes a much larger probability of a slow response overall.
concepts.title: Tail Latency Amplification

concepts.description: Separating "users see fresh state" from "state is never corrupt" — lag is temporary and tolerable, integrity violations are permanent, and dataflow systems can guarantee integrity without coordination.
concepts.title: Timeliness vs. Integrity

concepts.description: Timeouts are the only way to detect remote failure on an asynchronous network, and choosing them is a trade-off between slow detection and declaring live nodes dead.
concepts.title: Timeouts and Failure Detection

concepts.description: A protocol delivering every message to every node exactly once and in the same order — equivalent to consensus, and the foundation of state machine replication.
concepts.title: Total Order Broadcast

concepts.description: Aborts exist so transactions can be safely retried — but retrying correctly must handle duplicate effects, overload, and permanent errors.
concepts.title: Transaction Aborts and Retries

concepts.description: Writing a state change and its outgoing event in the same local database transaction, then relaying the event via change data capture, so a service never has to keep two systems consistent through separate writes.
concepts.title: Transactional Outbox Pattern

concepts.description: No node can trust its own perception of the system; authoritative decisions (node death, leadership) must come from a quorum majority.
concepts.title: Truth Defined by the Majority

concepts.description: The atomic commit protocol making multiple nodes commit or abort a transaction together — safe, but blocking: a crashed coordinator leaves participants in doubt, holding locks.
concepts.title: Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

concepts.description: Composing specialized storage systems into one coherent whole by connecting them with asynchronous event logs — database internals turned inside-out, with application code as derivation functions.
concepts.title: Unbundling the Database

concepts.description: Each node's quartz clock drifts and jumps; wall-clock timestamps cannot order events across nodes, and a clock reading is really an uncertainty interval.
concepts.title: Unreliable Clocks

concepts.description: Asynchronous packet networks give no delivery or latency guarantees; a sender that gets no response cannot tell what failed, or whether the request was actually processed.
concepts.title: Unreliable Networks

concepts.description: Per-replica version counters attached to values, letting a system decide whether two versions are ordered (overwrite) or concurrent (keep siblings).
concepts.title: Version Vectors

concepts.description: Storing every update to a key under a new monotonic version instead of overwriting in place, so clients can address a specific point in a key's history and readers never block writers.
concepts.title: Versioned Value

concepts.description: Ordering transactions by age instead of building a waiting-for graph, so lock conflicts resolve by aborting one side deterministically rather than deadlocking.
concepts.title: Wound-Wait and Wait-Die Deadlock Avoidance

concepts.description: Persisting every state change as an append-only log entry before applying it in memory, so a crashed process can replay the log to recover exactly the state it had promised.
concepts.title: Write-Ahead Log

concepts.description: Acknowledging writes from an in-memory buffer instead of the storage engine trades a bounded durability risk for a large cut in tail latency, and composes with replica quorums to bound that risk without slowing the write down.
concepts.title: Write Buffering for Latency

concepts.description: Strategies for handling concurrent writes to the same data in multi-leader and leaderless systems: avoidance, convergent rules, sibling merging, and automatic merge algorithms.
concepts.title: Write Conflict Resolution

concepts.description: Concurrent transactions each read a shared precondition, then write to different objects, jointly violating an invariant no single write breaks — the anomaly snapshot isolation cannot catch.
concepts.title: Write Skew and Phantoms

concepts.description: A finer availability frame than up/down: yield is the chance of getting an answer at all; harvest is how complete that answer is when parts of the system are down.
concepts.title: Yield and Harvest
